Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.
Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.

questions.stem: What is the bonus B?
What final score S does the participant receive?
Another participant has one fewer correct answer, three fewer wrong answers and the same bonus. What is that participant’s score?
By how many points does the first participant’s score exceed the second participant’s score?
questions.explanation: The scores are 73 and 72, so the first exceeds the second by 1 point.
The product is (3/2)(4/3)(5/4)(6/5). All intermediate factors cancel, leaving 6/2 = 3.

questions.stem: Evaluate Σ from k=1 to 10 of 1/[k(k+2)].
Simplify (10⁶ − 1)/999.

questions.explanation: Work from the innermost term: 1+1/1=2; then 1+1/2=3/2; then 1+2/3=5/3; then 1+3/5=8/5. Thus the value is 8/5.

questions.stem: Evaluate (9999² − 9997²)/4 without squaring either number.
For positive x, simplify √(x + 2√(x−1)) + √(x − 2√(x−1)), given x ≥ 2.
questions.explanation: Write x = (x−1)+1. The radicands are (√(x−1)+1)² and (√(x−1)−1)². Since x≥2, both square roots are nonnegative, and their sum is 2√(x−1).

questions.stem: What is a₃?
What is a₅?
questions.explanation: The terms are 2/1, 3/2, 5/3, 8/5 and 13/8. Therefore a₅ = 13/8.

questions.stem: What is the product a₁a₂a₃a₄?
questions.explanation: The factors telescope: (2/1)(3/2)(5/3)(8/5) = 8.

questions.stem: Find √1764.
Evaluate ∛4913.
What is the principal square root of 0.0081?
questions.explanation: 0.09²=0.0081, so the principal square root is 0.09.

questions.stem: Which perfect square is immediately greater than 200?
questions.explanation: 14²=196 and 15²=225. Therefore the next perfect square above 200 is 225.

questions.stem: A cube-shaped micro-volume is 0.001 cubic unit. What is its edge length?
questions.explanation: The edge is the cube root of the volume. Since 0.1³=0.001, the edge length is 0.1 unit.

questions.stem: What is √64 + ∛64?
questions.explanation: √64=8 and ∛64=4. Their sum is 12.

questions.stem: Find the positive number whose square is 529.
questions.explanation: 23²=529, so the positive number is 23.

questions.stem: What is the cube of ∛125?
questions.explanation: ∛125=5, and its cube is 125. Equivalently, cubing reverses taking the real cube root.

questions.stem: A square has area 324 cm². What is its side length?
questions.explanation: Side = √area = √324 = 18 cm.

questions.stem: What least positive integer must multiply 432 to make the product a perfect square?
questions.explanation: 432=2⁴×3³. The exponent of 3 is odd, so multiply by 3 to obtain 2⁴×3⁴, a perfect square.

questions.stem: What least positive integer must divide 675 so that the quotient is a perfect square?
questions.explanation: 675=3³×5². Dividing by 3 leaves 3²×5²=225, a perfect square.

questions.stem: Find the smallest integer greater than √150.
questions.explanation: 12²=144<150<169=13². Therefore √150 lies between 12 and13, and the smallest greater integer is 13.

questions.stem: How many positive integers have squares between 100 and 500, inclusive?
questions.explanation: Squares from 10²=100 through 22²=484 lie in the interval; 23²=529 is too large. Count=22−10+1=13.

questions.stem: The cube of a positive integer ends in 7. What must be the units digit of the integer?
questions.explanation: Among digits 0–9, only 3 has a cube ending in 7 because 3³=27. Thus the units digit is 3.

questions.stem: Evaluate √2025 − ∛729.
questions.explanation: √2025=45 and ∛729=9. Difference=36.

questions.stem: If √x = 7.5, what is x?
questions.explanation: Squaring both sides gives x=7.5²=56.25.

questions.stem: If ∛(2x+11)=5, find x.
questions.explanation: Cubing gives 2x+11=125, so 2x=114 and x=57.

questions.stem: A cube has volume 2744 cm³. Find its edge length.
questions.explanation: Edge=∛2744=14 cm because 14³=2744.

questions.stem: Find √(144×225) without first multiplying the two numbers.
What is the geometric mean of 16 and 81?
questions.explanation: Geometric mean=√(16×81)=4×9=36.

questions.stem: The square root of a number is increased by 3 and becomes 11. What is the number?
questions.explanation: √n+3=11 gives √n=8, hence n=64.

questions.stem: How many digits are there in √10¹⁸?
questions.explanation: √10¹⁸=10⁹, which is 1 followed by 9 zeros and therefore has 10 digits.

questions.stem: What is the nearest integer to √70?
questions.explanation: 8²=64 and 9²=81. √70≈8.37, so the nearest integer is 8.

questions.stem:
What is the positive integer n?

**Statement I:** n is a perfect square between 80 and 120.

**Statement II:** √n is an odd integer.
questions.explanation: Statement I allows only 81 and100. Statement II alone allows many values. Together, only 81 has an odd square root, so both statements together are sufficient.

options.label: Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Even both statements together are not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.

questions.stem: A positive number is both a perfect square and a perfect cube. Which is the least such number greater than 1?
questions.explanation: Such a number must be a perfect sixth power. The least is 2⁶=64.

questions.stem: What least number must be multiplied by 2⁵×3⁴×5³ to make the result both a perfect square and a perfect cube?
questions.explanation: To be both, every exponent must be a multiple of 6. Add exponents 1,2 and3 respectively, so multiply by 2×3²×5³=2250.

questions.stem: Find the greatest four-digit perfect square.
questions.explanation: √9999 lies between 99 and100, so the greatest integer root is99. Hence the greatest four-digit square is99²=9801.

questions.stem: How many perfect cubes lie strictly between 1000 and 10000?
questions.explanation: 10³=1000 and 21³=9261<10000<22³. Strictly above1000 gives roots11 through21, a total of11 cubes.

questions.stem: If √(x+9) − √x = 1 for x≥0, find x.
questions.explanation: √(x+9)=√x+1. Squaring gives x+9=x+1+2√x, so √x=4 and x=16.

questions.stem: Solve ∛(x+19) + ∛(x−8) = 5, given that both cube roots are integers.
questions.explanation: Let a=∛(x+19), b=∛(x−8). Then a+b=5 and a³−b³=27. Testing integer pairs summing to5, a=3,b=2 gives difference27. Thus x−8=8 and x=16.

questions.stem: The sum of the square roots of two consecutive perfect squares is 41. What is the smaller square?
questions.explanation: Let the roots be n and n+1. Then 2n+1=41, so n=20. The smaller square is20²=400.

questions.stem: A rectangular screen has area 432 cm², and its length is 3 times its width. Find the width.
questions.explanation: Let width=w. Then 3w²=432, so w²=144 and w=12 cm.

questions.stem: What is the integer part of √2 + √3 + √5 + √7?
questions.explanation: Approximate values are1.414,1.732,2.236,2.646; sum≈8.028. Its integer part is8.

questions.stem: Find the least positive integer n such that 360n is a perfect cube.
questions.explanation: 360=2³×3²×5. To make exponents multiples of3, multiply by3¹×5²=75. Then360×75=30³.

questions.stem: If a positive integer N has exactly three positive square roots among the integers x satisfying x²≤N, and N itself is a perfect square, what is the least possible N?
questions.explanation: Positive integer x with x²≤N are1 through√N. Exactly three such x means√N=3, so N=9.

questions.stem:
What is the positive value of x?

**Statement I:** √(x+5)=x−1.

**Statement II:** x<5.
questions.explanation: Statement I, with x≥1, gives x+5=(x−1)², so x²−3x−4=0 and x=4 or−1; domain leaves x=4. It is sufficient. Statement II alone is insufficient. Thus Statement I alone is sufficient.

options.label: Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.
Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Even both statements together are not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.

questions.stem: What is the side length of the square floor?
What is the edge length of the cube?
questions.explanation: Edge=∛3375=15 m because15³=3375.

questions.stem: What is the ratio of the floor side to the cube edge?
questions.explanation: The dimensions are45 m and15 m, so the ratio is3:1.

questions.stem: If the floor side is reduced to match the cube edge, by what factor does the square floor area decrease?
questions.explanation: Area scales as the square of side. The side falls from45 to15, a factor of3, so area falls by3²=9. The new area is one-ninth of the old.

questions.stem: Find the least perfect square divisible by 90.
questions.explanation: 90=2×3²×5. To make all exponents even, multiply by2×5=10, giving900=30².
Squaring gives 2x+14+2√((x+15)(x−1))=64, so √((x+15)(x−1))=25−x. Squaring again yields x²+14x−15=(25−x)²=x²−50x+625, hence64x=640 and x=10. It checks in the original equation.

questions.stem: The expression √(n+√(n²−1)) + √(n−√(n²−1)) is evaluated for n≥1. What is its value?
questions.explanation: Let the expression be E. Squaring, E²=2n+2√(n²−(n²−1))=2n+2. Since E>0, E=√(2n+2).

questions.stem: Find the least positive integer n such that n is a perfect square, n/18 is an integer, and n/18 is a perfect cube.
questions.explanation: Write n=18k³=2×3²×k³ and require square exponents. For prime2,1+3a must be even, least a=1. For prime3,2+3b must be even, least b=0. Thus k=2 and n=18×8=144, which is12².

questions.stem: How many integers n from 1 through 10,000 are simultaneously a perfect square or a perfect cube, counting numbers that are both only once?
questions.explanation: Squares:⌊√10000⌋=100. Cubes:⌊∛10000⌋=21. Both are sixth powers:⌊10000^(1/6)⌋=4 (1,64,729,4096). Inclusion–exclusion gives100+21−4=117.

questions.stem: What least multiplier makes 540 a perfect square?
questions.explanation: 540=2²×3³×5. For a square, odd exponents of3 and5 need one extra each, so A=3×5=15.

questions.stem: What least multiplier makes 540 a perfect cube?
questions.explanation: For a cube, exponents must be multiples of3. The exponent of2 needs one more and that of5 needs two more, so B=2×5²=50.

questions.stem: What is √(540A)?
questions.explanation: 540A=540×15=8100=90², so the square root is90.

questions.stem: What is ∛(540B)?
questions.explanation: 540B=540×50=27000=30³, so the cube root is30.

questions.stem: An investor owns 200 shares of face value ₹10 carrying an 8% dividend. What annual dividend is received?
questions.explanation: Dividend per share is 8% of ₹10 = ₹0.80. For 200 shares, income = ₹160.

questions.stem: How many shares quoted at ₹60 can be bought for ₹12,000, ignoring brokerage?
questions.explanation: Number of shares = investment/market price = 12,000/60 = 200.

questions.stem: A ₹100 face-value share pays 12% dividend and sells at ₹150. What is its current yield?
questions.explanation: Dividend per share = ₹12. Yield = 12/150×100 = 8%.

questions.stem: What is the market value of 500 shares quoted at ₹25 each?
A ₹100 share pays an 18% dividend and is bought at ₹120. Find the yield.
questions.explanation: Annual dividend = ₹18. Yield = 18/120×100 = 15%.

questions.stem: A company declares 12% dividend on 300 shares of face value ₹5. What is the total dividend?
A share quoted at ₹90 is purchased with 1% brokerage. What is the acquisition cost per share?
questions.explanation: Brokerage = 1% of ₹90 = ₹0.90. Cost = ₹90.90.

questions.stem: A share is sold at ₹80 with 0.5% brokerage deducted. What are the net proceeds per share?
A shareholder receives ₹900 when the dividend is ₹6 per share. How many shares are held?
questions.explanation: Shares = total dividend/dividend per share = 900/6 = 150.

questions.stem: A ₹100 face-value share is quoted at a 25% premium. What is its market price?
questions.explanation: Market price = 100+25% of 100 = ₹125.

questions.stem: An investor has ₹50,000 including 2% purchase brokerage. Approximately how many whole shares quoted at ₹125 can be bought?
questions.explanation: Cost per share = 125×1.02 = ₹127.50. 50,000/127.50 = 392.15, so at most 392 whole shares.

questions.stem: A ₹100 share paying 16% dividend is bought at ₹120 with ₹2 brokerage per share and later incurs ₹1.50 annual custody cost. What is the net income yield on acquisition cost?
questions.explanation: Net annual income = ₹16−₹1.50=₹14.50. Acquisition cost=₹122. Yield=14.5/122×100=11.8852%.

questions.stem: ₹40,000 invested in a ₹100 share paying 10% dividend at market price ₹80 gives the same income as what investment in a ₹100 share paying 12% at ₹150?
questions.explanation: First yield=10/80=12.5%. Second yield=12/150=8%. Required investment=40,000×12.5/8=₹62,500.

questions.stem: A share is bought at ₹75, pays ₹6 dividend, and is sold one year later at ₹90, ignoring brokerage. What is the one-year holding return?
questions.explanation: Gain = price gain ₹15 + dividend ₹6 = ₹21. Return = 21/75×100 = 28%.

questions.stem: At what market price should a ₹100 share paying 12% dividend be bought to obtain a 10% yield?
questions.explanation: Price = annual dividend/yield = 12/0.10 = ₹120.

questions.stem: A ₹100 share pays 15% dividend. How many shares are needed for annual income ₹2,400?
questions.explanation: Dividend per share=₹15. Required shares=2,400/15=160.

questions.stem: An investor owns four shares acquired at ₹120 each and buys one rights share at ₹80 for every four held. What is the average acquisition cost per share after exercising the right?
questions.explanation: Cost of five-share block = 4×120+80=₹560. Average=560/5=₹112.

questions.stem: An investor paid ₹30,000 for 300 shares and later received a 1-for-3 bonus issue. What is the average cost per share after the bonus?
questions.explanation: Bonus shares = 100, total shares=400; total cost stays ₹30,000. Average cost=₹75.

questions.stem: Which offers the higher yield: a ₹100 share paying 10% dividend at ₹80, or a ₹50 share paying 16% dividend at ₹64?
questions.explanation: First yield=₹10/₹80=12.5%. Second dividend=₹8 and yield=₹8/₹64=12.5%. The yields are equal.

options.label: The first offers twice the yield.
The second offers 3.5 percentage points more.
The first offers 2.5 percentage points more.

questions.stem: Two hundred fifty shares are sold at ₹84 with 1% brokerage deducted. What net amount is received?
questions.explanation: Net per share=84×0.99=₹83.16. Total proceeds=250×83.16=₹20,790.

questions.stem: An investor holds 800 shares of face value ₹10 paying 15% dividend. If 10% tax is withheld from the dividend, what cash income is received?
questions.explanation: Gross dividend=800×10×15%=₹1,200. After 10% withholding, cash=₹1,080.

questions.stem: A share pays a constant ₹9 dividend. Its market price falls from ₹120 to ₹90. By how many percentage points does current yield rise?
questions.explanation: Yield rises from 7.5% to 10%, an increase of 2.5 percentage points.

questions.stem: A portfolio contains 200 shares yielding ₹8 dividend each and 150 shares yielding ₹12 each. What is total annual dividend income?
A share is bought at ₹100 with ₹1 purchase brokerage. It pays ₹8 dividend. At what quoted selling price, with 1% selling brokerage, will the total return be 20% on acquisition cost?
questions.explanation: Acquisition cost=₹101; target total value=₹121.20. Net sale proceeds required=121.20−8=₹113.20. Quoted price=113.20/0.99=₹114.34.

questions.stem: A ₹100 face-value share quoted at ₹140 gives a 9% yield. What dividend rate does the company declare?
questions.explanation: Dividend per share=9% of ₹140=₹12.60. On face value ₹100, the dividend rate is 12.6%.

questions.stem:
What is the yield on a share?

**Statement I:** Its face value is ₹100 and dividend rate is 12%.

**Statement II:** Its market price is ₹150.
questions.explanation: Statement I gives dividend ₹12 but not purchase price; Statement II gives price but not income. Together yield=12/150×100=8%.

options.label: Even both statements together are not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.

questions.stem: A portfolio has 300 shares bought at ₹80 paying ₹10 each and 200 shares bought at ₹125 paying ₹15 each. What is the dividend yield on total cost?
questions.explanation: Total cost=₹49,000; income=₹6,000. Portfolio yield=6000/49000×100=12.2449%.

questions.stem: An investor sells 400 shares at ₹75 with 1% brokerage and reinvests all proceeds in another share quoted at ₹99 with 1% purchase brokerage. How many whole new shares can be bought?
questions.explanation: Net sale proceeds=400×75×0.99=₹29,700. Cost per new share=99×1.01=₹99.99. Whole shares=floor(29,700/99.99)=297.

questions.stem: Two hundred shares are bought at ₹100 with 1% brokerage, pay ₹8 dividend each, and are sold at ₹112 with 1% brokerage. What is the total percentage return?
₹1,00,000 is split between two shares yielding 12.5% and 8%. If the two investments generate equal annual income, how much is invested in the first share?
An investor buys 600 shares at ₹50. After a 1-for-5 bonus issue, all shares are sold at ₹45, with no brokerage. What is the capital-gain percentage on original cost?
questions.explanation: Bonus adds 120 shares, so 720 are sold for ₹32,400. Gain=₹2,400 on ₹30,000=8%.

questions.stem: A share trades at ₹150 before a 1-for-3 rights issue at ₹90. Ignoring market effects, what is the theoretical ex-rights price?
questions.explanation: Value of a four-share block after exercising =3×150+90=₹540. Average=₹135.

questions.stem: An investor owns 100 shares of face value ₹10 paying 20% dividend. After a 1-for-1 bonus, the company declares 15% dividend on the enlarged holding. By what percentage does the investor’s dividend income change?
questions.explanation: Old income=100×₹2=₹200. New income=200×₹1.50=₹300. Increase=50%.

questions.stem: Share A costs ₹100 and pays ₹12 dividend subject to 10% withholding. Share B costs ₹125 and pays ₹15 with no withholding. By how many percentage points does B’s net yield exceed A’s?
questions.explanation: A net yield=10.8/100=10.8%. B yield=15/125=12%. Difference=1.2 percentage points.

questions.stem: A share pays ₹18 annual dividend. To obtain a 12% yield on total acquisition cost with 2% brokerage, what maximum quoted price should an investor pay?
questions.explanation: Maximum total cost per share=18/0.12=₹150. If quoted price is P, 1.02P=150; P=₹147.06.

questions.stem: Five hundred shares are sold at ₹120 with 1% brokerage. All proceeds buy whole shares at ₹90 with 1% brokerage; the new share pays ₹10 dividend. What annual income results?
questions.explanation: Net proceeds=₹59,400; cost per new share=₹90.90; whole shares=653. Income=653×₹10=₹6,530.

questions.stem: A portfolio contains 100 shares paying ₹10 each, bought at ₹80, and 200 shares paying ₹6 each, bought at ₹x. If portfolio dividend yield is 10%, find x.
questions.explanation: Income=₹1,000+₹1,200=₹2,200. For 10% yield total cost=₹22,000. First holding cost=₹8,000, leaving ₹14,000 for 200 shares; x=₹70.

questions.stem: A 2-for-1 stock split halves face value and doubles the share count. If the dividend rate on the new face value remains numerically unchanged, what happens to total dividend income?
questions.explanation: Each new share has half the face value and therefore half the dividend, but there are twice as many shares. Total dividend income remains unchanged.

questions.stem: One hundred shares are bought at ₹50 with 2% brokerage. They pay ₹2 dividend each and are sold with 1% brokerage. What quoted sale price gives an overall break-even result?
questions.explanation: Acquisition cost=₹5,100; dividend=₹200, so required net sale proceeds=₹4,900. If sale quote is S, 100S×0.99=4,900; S=₹49.49.

questions.stem: A ₹100 share bought at par pays ₹9 dividend for one year and is redeemed at ₹110. What is the holding-period return?
questions.explanation: Total gain=₹9 dividend+₹10 redemption premium=₹19. Return=19%.

questions.stem:
How many shares does an investor own?

**Statement I:** Annual dividend income is ₹3,600.

**Statement II:** Each share has face value ₹100 and the declared dividend is 12%.
questions.explanation: Statement II gives ₹12 income per share but no total holding; Statement I gives total income. Together shares=3,600/12=300.

options.label: Even both statements together are not sufficient.
Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.

questions.stem: A share quoted at ₹200 costs 1% brokerage, pays ₹25 dividend, and has 20% tax withheld. What capital is needed to obtain ₹10,000 annual cash dividend?
questions.explanation: Net dividend per share=₹20, so 500 shares are needed. Acquisition cost per share=₹202; total capital=₹1,01,000.

questions.stem: Share A costs ₹102 including brokerage and pays ₹12 dividend; Share B costs ₹51 and pays ₹5. With ₹50,000, an investor must buy at least 200 B shares and only whole shares. What is the maximum annual dividend?
questions.explanation: Buy the minimum 200 B shares for ₹10,200. The remaining ₹39,800 buys floor(39,800/102)=390 A shares. Income=200×5+390×12=₹5,680.

questions.stem: An investor buys 300 shares at ₹80. A 1-for-2 bonus is issued; the enlarged holding pays ₹4 per share and is then sold at ₹60. Ignoring brokerage, what is total return on original cost?
questions.explanation: After bonus, holding=450. Sale proceeds=₹27,000; dividend=₹1,800; original cost=₹24,000. Gain=₹4,800, so return=20%.

questions.stem: Share A costs ₹120 and pays ₹15; Share B costs ₹80 and pays ₹8. What is the least capital needed to hold positive whole numbers of both so that dividend income from each holding is equal?
questions.explanation: Need 15a=8b. Smallest positive solution a=8, b=15. Capital=8×120+15×80=₹2,160.

questions.stem: A share trades at ₹120 cum-rights and offers one new share at ₹80 for every four held. Under theoretical pricing, what is the value of the entitlement attached to a block of four old shares?
questions.explanation: TERP=(4×120+80)/5=₹112. Value per old share’s right=120−112=₹8. For four shares, entitlement value=₹32.

questions.stem: What is the total acquisition cost of the portfolio?
questions.explanation: Alpha cost=₹30,300 and Beta cost=₹36,720. Total=₹67,020.

questions.stem: What total annual dividend is received?
questions.explanation: Alpha pays ₹2 per share, giving ₹800. Beta pays ₹12 per share, giving ₹3,600. Total=₹4,400.

questions.stem: What is the portfolio’s dividend yield on acquisition cost?
Using year-end market values and dividends, what is the one-year total return on acquisition cost?
questions.explanation: Year-end market value=₹67,800. Total value including dividends=₹72,200. Return=7.729%.

questions.stem: Simplify 2³ × 2⁵.
questions.explanation: For the same base, add exponents: 2^(3+5)=2⁸=256.

questions.stem: Evaluate 5⁰ + 3².
questions.explanation: Any nonzero number to power zero is1. Thus5⁰+3²=1+9=10.

questions.stem: Simplify √72.
Evaluate 27^(2/3).
questions.explanation: The cube root of27 is3; squaring gives9.

questions.stem: Write 2⁻³ as a positive fraction.
questions.explanation: A negative exponent takes the reciprocal:2⁻³=1/2³=1/8.

questions.stem: Simplify √50 − √8.
questions.explanation: √50=5√2 and√8=2√2. Their difference is3√2.

questions.stem: Which of the following is irrational?
questions.explanation: √7 is irrational because7 is not a perfect square. The other options are rational.

questions.stem: Evaluate (3²)³.
questions.explanation: A power raised to a power multiplies exponents:3^(2×3)=3⁶=729.

questions.stem: Simplify √3 × √12.
If 4ˣ=64, what is x?
Rationalize 1/(√5−2).

questions.explanation: This is a difference of squares:7−3=4.

questions.stem: A scaling factor is defined as the cube of the fourth root of 16. What is the factor?
questions.explanation: The fourth root of 16 is 2, and cubing that value gives 8.

questions.stem: If 2^(x+1)=32, find x.
questions.explanation: 32=2⁵, so x+1=5 and x=4.

questions.stem: Simplify √(5+2√6).
questions.explanation: Since (√3+√2)²=3+2+2√6=5+2√6, the principal square root is√3+√2.
The fourth roots of81 and16 are3 and2, so the value is3/2.

questions.stem: Simplify 3√12 + 2√27.
Find the value of (2⁷×4³)/8⁴.
questions.explanation: Write all terms in base2:2⁷×2⁶/2¹²=2¹=2.

questions.stem: Which is greater: √11 or 10/3?
questions.explanation: Both are positive. Squaring gives11 versus100/9≈11.111, so10/3 is greater.

questions.stem: If x^(1/2)=5 and x>0, find x^(3/2).
Rationalize 3/(2+√3).
questions.explanation: Multiply by2−√3. Since(2+√3)(2−√3)=1, the result is3(2−√3)=6−3√3.
The factors are3,3 and2, so their product is18.

questions.stem: If a=√5+2, what is 1/a?
questions.explanation: Because(√5+2)(√5−2)=1, the reciprocal is√5−2.

questions.stem: Simplify (x³y⁻²)/(x⁻¹y), for nonzero x and y.
questions.explanation: Subtract exponents on division: x^(3−(−1))y^(−2−1)=x⁴y⁻³=x⁴/y³.

questions.stem:
What is the value of 2ˣ?

**Statement I:** 4ˣ=64.

**Statement II:** x is a positive integer.
questions.explanation: Statement I gives2^(2x)=2⁶, so x=3 and2ˣ=8; it is sufficient. Statement II alone is insufficient. Thus Statement I alone is sufficient.

options.label: Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Even both statements together are not sufficient.

questions.stem: If √a=2√3 and a>0, find a.
questions.explanation: Squaring gives a=(2√3)²=4×3=12.

questions.stem: Simplify √(9−4√5).
questions.explanation: Seek√m−√n with m+n=9 and2√(mn)=4√5, so mn=20. The pair is5 and4. Hence the value is√5−2.

questions.stem: If a=2+√3, find a²+1/a².
questions.explanation: Since1/a=2−√3, a+1/a=4. Therefore a²+1/a²=(a+1/a)²−2=16−2=14.

questions.stem: Rationalize 1/(√2+√3+√5).
questions.explanation: Multiply by √2+√3−√5. The denominator becomes (√2+√3)²−5=2√6. Multiplying numerator and denominator by √6 gives (2√3+3√2−√30)/12.
27=3³, so exponents satisfy2x−1=3x−6. Hence x=5.

questions.stem: Evaluate (√2+1)⁴ + (√2−1)⁴.
questions.explanation: Let u=√2+1 and v=√2−1. Then u+v=2√2, uv=1. u²+v²=(u+v)²−2uv=8−2=6. Therefore u⁴+v⁴=(u²+v²)²−2u²v²=36−2=34.

questions.stem: If x=∛2+∛4, what is x³?
questions.explanation: Let a=∛2, so x=a+a². Then x³=a³(1+a)³=2(1+3a+3a²+a³)=6+6∛2+6∛4.

questions.stem: Find x if 8ˣ×4^(1−x)=32.
questions.explanation: Using base2,2^(3x)×2^(2−2x)=2^(x+2)=2⁵. Hence x=3.
Multiply numerator and denominator by√7+√5. The denominator is2; numerator is12+2√35. The result is6+√35.
Square the given relation:4ˣ+4^(−x)+2=25/4. Thus the required sum is25/4−2=17/4.

questions.stem: For positive a and b, simplify (a^(1/2)−b^(1/2))/(a−b), assuming a≠b.
questions.explanation: Since a−b=(√a−√b)(√a+√b), cancellation gives1/(√a+√b).

questions.stem:
What is the value of x, where x>0?

**Statement I:** x^(1/2)+x^(−1/2)=3.

**Statement II:** x>1.
questions.explanation: Statement I gives t+1/t=3 for t=√x, producing reciprocal solutions t=(3±√5)/2 and hence two reciprocal x-values. Statement II selects the solution t>1 and therefore a unique x. Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.

options.label: Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Even both statements together are not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.

questions.stem: What is pq?
What is p+q?
questions.explanation: The√2 terms cancel, leaving2√3.

questions.stem: What is p²+q²?
What is p³+q³?
If a^m=8 and a^n=32 for a>0, a≠1, what is m/n?
questions.explanation: Dividing logarithms, m/n=log_a8/log_a32. Since8=2³ and32=2⁵, the ratio is3/5.

questions.stem: Solve 2ˣ + 2^(1−x) = 3 for real x.
questions.explanation: Let t=2ˣ>0. Then2^(1−x)=2/t. The equation t+2/t=3 gives t²−3t+2=0, so t=1 or2. Hence x=0 or1.
The radicands are (2+√3)² and(2−√3)². Their principal roots are2+√3 and2−√3; the difference is2√3.

questions.stem: Find the least positive integer n such that 12ⁿ is both a perfect square and a perfect cube.
questions.explanation: 12ⁿ=2^(2n)3ⁿ. For a sixth power, both exponents must be multiples of6. Thus n must be a multiple of6; the least is6.

questions.stem: If x=√2+√3, simplify x⁶−10x⁴+x².
questions.explanation: x²=5+2√6. Let y=x². Since y and1/y=5−2√6 satisfy y+1/y=10, y²−10y+1=0. Multiplying by y gives y³−10y²+y=0, which is exactly the expression. Hence the value is0.

questions.stem: What is S₁?
What is S₂?
What recurrence relates Sₙ₊₁, Sₙ and Sₙ₋₁?
questions.explanation: Multiplying Sₙ by u+u⁻¹=4 gives uⁿ⁺¹+uⁿ⁻¹+u⁻ⁿ⁺¹+u⁻ⁿ⁻¹=Sₙ₊₁+Sₙ₋₁. Therefore Sₙ₊₁=4Sₙ−Sₙ₋₁.

questions.stem: What is S₄?
A student travels 150 km in 3 hours. What is the average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed=distance/time=150/3=50 km/h.

questions.stem: How far does a shuttle moving at 72 km/h travel in 25 minutes?
questions.explanation: 25 minutes=5/12 hour. Distance=72×5/12=30 km.

questions.stem: How long does a vehicle take to cover 180 km at 60 km/h?
questions.explanation: Time=180/60=3 hours.

questions.stem: Convert 54 km/h to metres per second.
questions.explanation: Multiply by 5/18: 54×5/18=15 m/s.

questions.stem: Convert 20 m/s to kilometres per hour.
questions.explanation: Multiply by 18/5: 20×18/5=72 km/h.

questions.stem: A cyclist covers 24 km at 16 km/h. How many minutes does the trip take?
questions.explanation: Time=24/16=1.5 hours=90 minutes.

questions.stem: Two robots start 100 m apart and move toward each other at 3 m/s and 2 m/s. After how many seconds do they meet?
questions.explanation: Relative speed=5 m/s. Time=100/5=20 seconds.

questions.stem: A bus covers half of a 120 km route. How much distance remains?
questions.explanation: Half of 120 km is 60 km, so 60 km remains.

questions.stem: A runner increases speed from 10 km/h to 12 km/h. What is the percentage increase?
questions.explanation: Increase=2 on base 10, so 2/10×100=20%.

questions.stem: A cab leaves at 8:15 AM and arrives at 10:45 AM. What is the travel duration?
questions.explanation: From 8:15 to 10:45 is 2 hours 30 minutes.

questions.stem: A car travels equal distances at 40 km/h and 60 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole journey?
questions.explanation: For equal distances, average speed is harmonic mean: 2×40×60/(40+60)=48 km/h.

questions.stem: A delivery van travels for 2 hours at 60 km/h and 3 hours at 80 km/h. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Total distance=120+240=360 km; total time=5 hours. Average=72 km/h.

questions.stem: Two cars start simultaneously from towns 240 km apart and drive toward each other at 60 km/h and 20 km/h. When do they meet?
questions.explanation: Closing speed=80 km/h. Time=240/80=3 hours.

questions.stem: A car moving at 70 km/h starts 180 km behind a truck moving in the same direction at 40 km/h. How long does the car take to catch it?
questions.explanation: Relative speed=30 km/h. Catch-up time=180/30=6 hours.

questions.stem: How much time is saved on a 300 km journey when speed rises from 50 km/h to 75 km/h?
questions.explanation: Times are 6 hours and 4 hours; saving=2 hours.

questions.stem: A bus has an overall speed of 45 km/h including a 15-minute stop in every hour. What is its running speed?
questions.explanation: It moves for 45 minutes per clock hour. Running speed×0.75=45, so running speed=60 km/h.

questions.stem: A commuter is 120 minutes late at 40 km/h and 60 minutes late at 60 km/h for the same trip. What is the route distance?
questions.explanation: Difference in travel times is 1 hour. D(1/40−1/60)=1, giving D=120 km.

questions.stem: An express bus leaves 2 hours after a coach that travels at 60 km/h. If the express moves at 90 km/h, how many hours after its own departure does it catch the coach?
questions.explanation: Coach head start=120 km. Relative speed=30 km/h. Catch-up time=4 hours.

questions.stem: Two cyclists start from the same point in opposite directions at 30 km/h and 20 km/h. After how many hours are they 120 km apart?
questions.explanation: Separation speed=50 km/h. Time=120/50=2.4 hours.

questions.stem: For a fixed distance, A’s speed is 25% greater than B’s. What is the ratio of their travel times A:B?
questions.explanation: Speed ratio A:B=1.25:1=5:4. Time ratio is inverse, 4:5.

questions.stem: A bus travelling at 60 km/h stops for 10 minutes. At what speed must it travel afterward to recover the lost time over the next 30 km?
questions.explanation: At 60 km/h, 30 km takes 30 minutes. To recover 10 minutes, it must take 20 minutes, so required speed=30/(1/3)=90 km/h.

questions.stem: Two runners start together from the same point on a 600 m circular track in opposite directions at 4 m/s and 6 m/s. When do they first meet?
questions.explanation: Relative speed=10 m/s. Time=600/10=60 seconds.

questions.stem: On a 400 m track, two runners start together in the same direction at 7 m/s and 5 m/s. When does the faster first lap the slower?
questions.explanation: Relative speed=2 m/s. Lap time=400/2=200 seconds.

questions.stem: A 200 km route is covered 40% at 40 km/h and the remainder at 80 km/h. What is the average speed?
questions.explanation: Times: 80/40=2 hours and 120/80=1.5 hours. Average=200/3.5=57.1429 km/h.

questions.stem: A journey takes 90 minutes longer at 4 km/h than at 6 km/h. What is the distance?
questions.explanation: Time difference=1.5 h. D(1/4−1/6)=1.5, so D=18 km.

questions.stem:
What is the distance between two towns?

**Statement I:** A car takes 3 hours at constant speed.

**Statement II:** Its speed is 60 km/h.
questions.explanation: Time alone or speed alone is insufficient. Together distance=60×3=180 km.

options.label: Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.
Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Even both statements together are not sufficient.

questions.stem: A route is split into three equal-distance sections travelled at 30, 45, and 90 km/h. What is the overall average speed?
questions.explanation: For equal distances, average=3/(1/30+1/45+1/90)=45 km/h.

questions.stem: A candidate reaches an exam centre 30 minutes late at 48 km/h but 15 minutes early at 60 km/h. What is the distance to the centre?
questions.explanation: Travel-time difference=45 minutes=0.75 hour. D(1/48−1/60)=0.75, so D=180 km.

questions.stem: Two travellers start simultaneously from opposite ends. After meeting, A needs 4 hours to finish and B needs 9 hours. What is speed ratio A:B?
questions.explanation: For simultaneous starts, post-meeting times are inversely proportional to squared speeds: vA/vB=√(9/4)=3/2.

questions.stem: A truck travels at 50 km/h. A car starts 2 hours later at 70 km/h, but after 2 hours of pursuit increases to 90 km/h. How long after the car starts does it catch the truck?
questions.explanation: Initial gap=100 km. First 2 pursuit hours close 40 km, leaving 60. New relative speed=40 km/h, requiring 1.5 hours. Total=3.5 hours.

questions.stem: A 300 km trip consists of 120 km at 60 km/h, a 15-minute halt, then 180 km at 90 km/h. What is the overall elapsed time?
questions.explanation: Travel times are 2 h and 2 h, plus 0.25 h halt. Total=4.25 hours.

questions.stem: A driver plans to cover 300 km at 60 km/h. The first 120 km is covered at only 40 km/h. What speed is required for the remaining distance to arrive on schedule?
questions.explanation: Scheduled time=5 h. First part takes 3 h, leaving 2 h for 180 km. Required speed=90 km/h.

questions.stem: A person takes 90 seconds to walk along a stationary moving walkway and 60 seconds when walking at the same pace while it runs. How long would the walkway take to carry a standing person?
questions.explanation: Let length L. Walking speed=L/90. Combined speed=L/60, so walkway speed=L/60−L/90=L/180. Standing time=180 seconds.

questions.stem: A 240 km journey is covered half at 60 km/h and half at 80 km/h, with a 30-minute stop between segments. What is overall average speed including the stop?
questions.explanation: Times=2 h+1.5 h+0.5 h=4 h. Average=240/4=60 km/h.

questions.stem: Three runners start together on a 360 m track in the same direction at 3, 4, and 5 m/s. After how many seconds are all together again at the starting point?
questions.explanation: Their lap times are 120, 90, and 72 seconds. LCM(120,90,72)=360 seconds.

questions.stem: Two vehicles start from opposite ends of a 300 km route. Initially their speeds are 40 and 60 km/h. If the first speed rises to 50 km/h while the second stays 60, how far does the meeting point shift from the first vehicle’s end?
questions.explanation: Original meeting distance=300×40/100=120 km. New=300×50/110=136.3636 km. Shift=16.3636 km.

questions.stem: A relay vehicle covers consecutive legs of 120 km at 40 km/h, 100 km at 50 km/h, and 140 km at 70 km/h. What is overall average speed?
questions.explanation: Times=3+2+2=7 h; distance=360 km. Average=360/7=51.4286 km/h.

questions.stem: A bus can travel a route at 40 km/h with a 30-minute stop, or without stopping at 30 km/h, taking the same total time. What is the route length?
For a fixed journey, travel time is reduced by 20%. By what percentage must speed increase?
questions.explanation: New time=0.8 old time, so new speed=1/0.8=1.25 old speed. Increase=25%.

questions.stem: A leaves town X at 60 km/h. One hour later B leaves town Y toward X at 90 km/h. They meet 3 hours after A started. What is distance XY?
questions.explanation: A covers 60×3=180 km; B travels 2 hours and covers 180 km. Total=360 km.

questions.stem:
What is a car’s average speed for a journey?

**Statement I:** It covers the first half of the distance at 40 km/h.

**Statement II:** It covers the second half at 60 km/h.
questions.explanation: For equal halves, both speeds are needed; together average=2×40×60/(40+60)=48 km/h. Neither alone suffices.

options.label: Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Even both statements together are not sufficient.

questions.stem: A car gives 12 km/L at 60 km/h and 10 km/L at 80 km/h. It covers 120 km at each speed. What is its overall fuel efficiency?

A and B start simultaneously from opposite ends of a 300 km road at 60 and 40 km/h, reverse immediately on reaching the opposite end, and continue. How far from A’s starting end do they meet for the second time?
questions.explanation: First meeting is after 3 h. A reaches B’s end at 5 h; B reaches A’s end at 7.5 h. At 7.5 h A is 150 km from B’s end, hence 150 km from A’s end. They approach at 100 km/h and meet 1.5 h later. A has then moved another 90 km toward its start, meeting 60 km from A’s end.

questions.stem: A 400 km autonomous-vehicle test must finish in 5 hours. The first 100 km is limited to 50 km/h and the last 100 km to at most 100 km/h. What minimum constant speed is required on the middle 200 km?
questions.explanation: First segment uses 2 h. To minimize middle speed, use maximum 100 km/h on last segment, taking 1 h. Two hours remain for 200 km, requiring 100 km/h.

questions.stem: A truck has an 80 km lead and moves at 40 km/h. A chase vehicle moves at 60 km/h but must stop for 10 minutes after each completed hour of driving. How long after the chase begins is the truck caught?
questions.explanation: Each full drive-plus-stop cycle reduces the gap by 20−40/6=13⅓ km. After five such cycles, 13⅓ km remains and 5⅚ h have elapsed. At 20 km/h relative speed, the final catch takes 2/3 h. Total=6.5 h.

questions.stem: On a 300 km route, the first 120 km can be driven at 60 km/h before 8 AM but only 40 km/h afterward; the remaining 180 km can be driven at 90 km/h before 10 AM but only 60 km/h afterward. Compare departures at 7 AM and 8 AM. How much earlier does the 7 AM departure arrive?
questions.explanation: Leaving 7: first leg ends 9; second leg covers 90 km by 10 and 90 km in 1.5 h, arriving 11:30. Leaving 8: first leg takes 3 h and second 3 h, arriving 2 PM. Difference=2.5 hours.

questions.stem: How long does the outward trip take, including the stop?
What is the outward-trip average speed including the stop?
questions.explanation: Average speed=210/4=52.5 km/h.

questions.stem: How long does the return trip take including its stop?
questions.explanation: Running time=210/70=3 hours; with a 30-minute stop, elapsed time=3.5 hours.

questions.stem: What is the average speed for the complete round trip, including all stops?
questions.explanation: Total distance=420 km and total time=4+3.5=7.5 hours. Average=56 km/h.

questions.stem: A can complete a coding task in 12 days and B in 18 days. Working together at constant rates, how many days will they take?
questions.explanation: Combined rate = 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 task/day. Time = 36/5 = 7.2 days.

questions.stem: A technician can install a system in 20 hours. What fraction of the work is completed in 5 hours?
questions.explanation: At a constant rate, completed fraction = 5/20 = 1/4.

questions.stem: A and B together finish a job in 10 days. A alone takes 15 days. How long would B alone take?
questions.explanation: B’s rate = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30 job/day, so B takes 30 days.

questions.stem: Six identical machines complete a batch in 24 hours. How many machine-hours are required per machine if 24 identical machines share the same batch equally?
questions.explanation: Total machine-hours = 6×24 = 144. With 24 machines, time = 144/24 = 6 hours.

questions.stem: Sixteen workers complete a landscaping job in 15 days. At the same productivity, how many days would 20 workers need?
questions.explanation: Workers×days is constant: 16×15 = 20×d. Thus d = 12 days.

questions.stem: A team completes 25% of a project each week. How many weeks does the project take at that rate?
questions.explanation: Time = 100%/25% per week = 4 weeks.

questions.stem: Machine X is 50% more efficient than Machine Y. If Y needs 30 hours for a job, how long does X need?
questions.explanation: X’s rate is 1.5 times Y’s, so its time is 30/1.5 = 20 hours.

questions.stem: Nine developers can finish a module in 8 days. How many days will 12 equally productive developers take?
questions.explanation: Developer-days = 9×8 = 72. Time with 12 developers = 72/12 = 6 days.

questions.stem: A contractor can finish a job in 8 days. What percentage of the job remains after working alone for 3 days?
questions.explanation: Completed = 3/8. Remaining = 5/8 = 62.5%.

questions.stem: Two workers complete a job together and are paid ₹4,800 in proportion to their work rates, which are 3:5. What is the slower worker’s share?
questions.explanation: The slower worker gets 3 of 8 parts: 4800×3/8 = ₹1,800.

questions.stem: A can finish a project in 12 days and B in 18 days. A works alone for 3 days, after which B joins. How many days from the start will the project take?
questions.explanation: A completes 3/12 = 1/4. Remaining 3/4 at combined rate 5/36 takes (3/4)/(5/36)=5.4 days. Total = 8.4 days.

questions.stem: A and B can finish a job alone in 10 and 15 days. They work together for 4 days, then A leaves. How many days in total are required?
questions.explanation: Together they complete 4×(1/10+1/15)=2/3. B completes the remaining 1/3 in 5 days. Total = 9 days.

questions.stem: A completes a task in 12 days and B in 16 days. What is the ratio of their efficiencies A:B?
questions.explanation: Efficiency is inverse to time, so A:B = 1/12:1/16 = 16:12 = 4:3.

questions.stem: Three engineers have the same daily output as five trainees. If 12 engineers complete a task in 10 days, how many days will 10 trainees take?
questions.explanation: Ten trainees are equivalent to 10×3/5 = 6 engineers. Total work = 12×10 engineer-days. Time = 120/6 = 20 days.

questions.stem: Twenty workers are scheduled to finish a job in 15 days. After 5 days, the scope increases by 25% of the original job, with workforce unchanged. How many total days are needed?
questions.explanation: In 5 days they complete 1/3 of the original job. New total work is 1.25, so remaining = 1.25−1/3 = 11/12. At rate 1/15 job/day, this takes 13.75 days. Total = 18.75 days.

questions.stem: A can finish a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. They work on alternate days, starting with A. How long will the job take?
questions.explanation: In each two-day cycle they complete 1/10+1/15 = 1/6. Five cycles complete 5/6 in 10 days. Day 11 by A raises completion to 14/15; B finishes the last 1/15 on day 12.

questions.stem: A developer can finish a module in 20 days. After working for 8 days, automation doubles the developer’s productivity. How many days in total are needed?
questions.explanation: First 8 days complete 8/20 = 40%. Remaining 60% at double rate (1/10 per day) takes 6 days. Total = 14 days.

questions.stem: Worker A is twice as efficient as a standard worker and works 6 days. Worker B is three times as efficient and works 4 days. In what ratio should wages be divided?
questions.explanation: Work contributions are 2×6 = 12 and 3×4 = 12. Wage ratio = 1:1.

questions.stem: Thirty workers can finish a project in 20 days. After 8 days, six workers leave. How many days from the start will the project take?
questions.explanation: Total work = 600 worker-days. Work done = 30×8 = 240. Remaining = 360 worker-days, completed by 24 workers in 15 days. Total = 23 days.

questions.stem: Eight machines working 12 hours per day complete a batch in 5 days. How many days will ten identical machines working 8 hours per day require?
questions.explanation: Total machine-hours = 8×12×5 = 480. New daily capacity = 10×8 = 80 machine-hours. Days = 480/80 = 6.

questions.stem: A completes 2/5 of a job in 6 days, while B completes the remaining 3/5 in 9 days when working alone. If they work together from the start, how long will the full job take?
questions.explanation: A’s full-job time = 6÷(2/5)=15 days. B’s full-job time = 9÷(3/5)=15 days. Together they take 15/2 = 7.5 days.

questions.stem: Five senior technicians have the same output as eight juniors. A team of 10 seniors and 16 juniors completes a job in 12 days. If 5 seniors are replaced by 8 juniors, how many days will the job take?
questions.explanation: The replacement preserves equivalent capacity because 5 seniors = 8 juniors. Therefore completion time remains 12 days.

questions.stem: Two teams can complete a task alone in 18 and 27 days. What percentage of the task do they complete together in 5 days?
questions.explanation: Combined rate = 1/18+1/27 = 5/54. In 5 days they complete 25/54 = 46.2963%.

questions.stem: Twenty-four workers can finish a task in 18 days. After 6 days, management wants the task completed in 8 more days. How many workers in total are needed for the remaining work?
questions.explanation: Total work = 24×18 = 432 worker-days. Done = 24×6 = 144; remaining = 288. Required workforce = 288/8 = 36 workers.

questions.stem: A machine is scheduled to finish a job in 12 days. After 4 days, its productivity falls by 25%. How many days in total will it take?
questions.explanation: First 4 days complete 1/3. New rate = 75% of 1/12 = 1/16. Remaining 2/3 takes 32/3 = 10.6667 days. Total = 14.6667 days.

questions.stem:
How many days will A take to complete a job alone?

**Statement I:** A and B together take 8 days.

**Statement II:** B alone takes 24 days.
questions.explanation: Neither statement alone gives A’s rate. Together, A’s rate = 1/8−1/24 = 1/12, so A takes 12 days. Both statements together are sufficient.

options.label: Even both statements together are not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.
Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.

questions.stem: A, B and C can finish a task in 12, 18 and 36 days. They work one day each in the repeating order A–B–C. How long is required?
questions.explanation: Each 3-day cycle completes 1/12+1/18+1/36 = 1/6. Five cycles complete 5/6 in 15 days. A completes 1/12 on day 16, leaving 1/12; B needs (1/12)/(1/18)=1.5 days. Total = 17.5 days.

questions.stem: A and B together take 10 days, B and C take 12 days, and C and A take 15 days. How long do all three take together?
questions.explanation: Adding pair rates gives 2(A+B+C) = 1/10+1/12+1/15 = 1/4. Thus all-three rate = 1/8 and time = 8 days.

questions.stem: A+B finish in 10 days, A+C in 15 days, and B+C in 30 days. How many days does A alone require?

A project requires 70 standard worker-days. Six workers start, and two additional workers join at the beginning of each subsequent day. Assuming productivity is continuous, when is the project completed?
questions.explanation: Work in first six days = 6+8+10+12+14+16 = 66 worker-days. On day 7 there are 18 workers; 4 worker-days need 4/18 = 2/9 day. Total = 6.2222 days.

questions.stem: A technician must assemble 100 units. The first 40 are assembled at 5 per day; after learning, productivity rises by 50%. How many days are required in total?
questions.explanation: First 40 take 8 days. New rate = 7.5 per day; remaining 60 take 8 days. Total = 16 days.

questions.stem: A worker completes 1/10 of a job per day. At the end of every incomplete day, a fault destroys 1/40 of the total job already completed that day. On which day is the job first completed?
questions.explanation: On each incomplete day net progress is 1/10−1/40 = 3/40. After 12 days, 36/40 = 0.9 is complete. On day 13 the worker adds 0.1 and completes the job before any destruction occurs.

questions.stem: Team A can finish a task in 15 days working 8 hours daily. Team B can finish it in 20 days working 6 hours daily. If both work together for 10 hours daily at their respective hourly rates, how many days will they need?
questions.explanation: A and B each require 120 team-hours, so each hourly rate is 1/120. Together for 10 hours they complete 20/120 = 1/6 per day. Time = 6 days.

questions.stem: Forty workers working 8 hours daily can finish a job in 15 days. In a revised plan, 10% are absent; the rest work 10 hours daily but at 90% of normal hourly efficiency. How many days are required?
questions.explanation: Original work = 40×8×15 standard worker-hours. Revised daily effective work = 36×10×0.9 = 324. Time = 4800/324 = 14.8148 days.

questions.stem: A starts a job alone and works 4 days. B then joins, and they finish in 5 more days. A alone would take 12 days. In what ratio should the total wage be divided between A and B?
questions.explanation: A works 9 days, contributing 9/12 = 3/4 of the job. B contributes the remaining 1/4. Wage ratio A:B = 3:1.

questions.stem: A team planned to finish a project in 20 days, but after 8 days only 30% is complete. To finish in the next 10 days, by what percentage must its current daily productivity increase?
questions.explanation: Current daily rate = 30%/8 = 3.75% of job. Required rate = 70%/10 = 7%. Increase = (7/3.75−1)×100 = 86.6667%.

questions.stem: Twenty workers can finish a job in 20 days. After 5 days, five leave; after another 5 days, ten workers join the reduced team. When is the job completed?
questions.explanation: Total work = 400 worker-days. First phase does 100; second phase does 15×5 = 75. Remaining 225 is done by 25 workers in 9 days. Total = 5+5+9 = 19 days.

questions.stem: A project splits into two independent modules containing 60% and 40% of the total work. Team A could complete the entire project in 12 days; Team B could complete the entire project in 10 days. They work in parallel on their assigned modules. When is the project finished?
questions.explanation: Team A needs 0.60×12 = 7.2 days. Team B needs 0.40×10 = 4 days. The project completes when the slower module finishes: 7.2 days.

questions.stem: A is twice as efficient as B, while C is half as efficient as B. Together they finish a task in 8 days. How long would A alone take?
questions.explanation: Let B’s rate be r. Total rate = 2r+r+0.5r = 3.5r = 1/8, so r=1/28. A’s rate = 1/14, hence A takes 14 days.

questions.stem:
How many days will A and B together take?

**Statement I:** A is 50% more efficient than B.

**Statement II:** A alone takes 12 days.
questions.explanation: Statement I gives only a relative rate. Statement II gives only A. Together, B’s rate is (2/3) of A’s: A=1/12, B=1/18, combined=5/36, so time=7.2 days. Both are required.

options.label: Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.
Even both statements together are not sufficient.
Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.

questions.stem: Eighteen workers can finish a job in 24 days. After 8 days, what is the minimum integer workforce required to finish the job by the end of day 18?
questions.explanation: Total work = 432 worker-days; 144 are done, leaving 288. Ten days remain. Required workers = 288/10 = 28.8, so at least 29 workers are needed.

questions.stem: A machine’s nominal completion time is 15 days. It works at full efficiency for 3 days, at 80% efficiency for 5 days, and then at 120% efficiency. When does it finish?
questions.explanation: Work done = 3/15 + 5×0.8/15 = 7/15. Remaining = 8/15. At rate 1.2/15 = 2/25 per day, remaining time = (8/15)/(2/25)=6.6667 days. Total = 14.6667 days.

questions.stem: A+B complete a job in 8 days, B+C in 12 days, and all three together in 6 days. How long would A alone take?
questions.explanation: A’s rate = all-three rate − (B+C) rate = 1/6−1/12 = 1/12. Therefore A takes 12 days.

questions.stem: A works on odd-numbered days and B on even-numbered days. A alone needs 8 days and B alone 12 days. On every third calendar day, whoever works produces only half their normal daily output. Starting with A on day 1, when is the task completed?
questions.explanation: The six-day pattern contributes 1/8+1/12+1/16+1/12+1/8+1/24 = 25/48. After one cycle, 25/48 is done. Continuing the same rates, completion occurs after 11 days.

questions.stem: A team can complete 20% of a project per week. At the end of every incomplete week, quality review invalidates 10% of all work completed up to that point. Assuming work is continuous within a week, when is the project first completed?
questions.explanation: Let completed work after review be x. The recurrence is x_new=0.9(x+0.2). Iterating gives the start-of-week balances until the final week; the project reaches 100% after 6.783 weeks, before that week’s review.

questions.stem: Two independent modules must be assigned one each to A and B. A would take 6 days for Module X and 10 for Y; B would take 8 days for X and 12 for Y. If they work in parallel, what is the minimum project completion time?
questions.explanation: Assignment A→X, B→Y finishes in max(6,12)=12 days. Assignment A→Y, B→X finishes in max(10,8)=10 days. Minimum = 10 days.

questions.stem: How many task-points are completed in the first 10 days?
questions.explanation: Daily output initially = 8×6 + 6×5 = 78 task-points. In 10 days, output = 780.

questions.stem: How many task-points remain immediately before automation is introduced?
questions.explanation: After reassignment, daily output = 6×6+6×5 = 66. Five-day output = 330. Total completed = 780+330 = 1,110, so 90 remain.

questions.stem: How many days after automation is introduced are needed to finish the migration?
questions.explanation: Post-automation rate = 66×1.20 = 79.2 task-points/day. Time for 90 points = 90/79.2 = 1.1364 days.

questions.stem: What is the total migration duration from the start?
questions.explanation: Fifteen full days elapse before automation, followed by 1.1364 days. Total = 16.1364 days.

questions.stem: What is the true discount on ₹22,000 due after one year at 10% simple interest?
A sum of ₹32,400 is due in one year. Find its present worth at 8% simple interest.
The present worth of a bill due in 6 months is ₹25,000. At 12% per annum, what is its true discount?
questions.explanation: True discount equals interest on present worth: 25,000×12%×0.5 = ₹1,500.

questions.stem: A one-year bill has amount due ₹51,500 and present worth ₹50,000. What simple-interest rate is implied?
The true discount on ₹26,000 at 10% per annum is ₹1,000. How many months remain until payment?
questions.explanation: Present worth=₹25,000. Since TD=PW×r×t, t=1,000/(25,000×0.10)=0.4 year=4.8 months.

questions.stem: At 9% simple interest, what sum due after 8 months has a present worth of ₹40,000?
Find the true discount on a ₹50,000 payment due in 6 months at 6%.
The true discount on a one-year amount is ₹2,400 and its present worth is ₹30,000. What is the rate?
questions.explanation: TD is simple interest on present worth: rate=2,400/30,000×100=8%.

questions.stem: A payment of ₹12,000 due later has a current present worth of ₹10,000. What is its true discount?
questions.explanation: True discount = amount due−present worth = ₹2,000.

questions.stem: A three-month obligation has present worth ₹18,000 at 10% per annum. What is the true discount?
A ₹48,000 vendor payment is due in 6 months. At 10%, how much rebate is mathematically equivalent to settling it today?
questions.explanation: The equivalent rebate is the true discount: 48,000×0.05/1.05 = ₹2,285.71.

questions.stem: The true discount on a nine-month bill at 9% is ₹1,800. Find the sum due.
A contractual payment of ₹90,000 is due after 18 months. What is its present worth at 8% simple interest?
For a nine-month bill evaluated at 12%, true discount is what percentage of present worth?
Two payments have the same present worth of ₹50,000 at 10%. One is due in 6 months and the other in 15 months. How much larger is the later amount due?
questions.explanation: Difference in amounts = PW×r×difference in time = 50,000×0.10×0.75 = ₹3,750.

questions.stem: A ₹60,000 amount is due in one year at an 8% valuation rate. If ₹20,000 is paid today, what additional present-value amount remains to be settled today?
questions.explanation: Full present worth=60,000/1.08=₹55,555.56. After ₹20,000, remaining present value=₹35,555.56.

questions.stem: At 10% simple interest, ₹34,500 due later has present worth ₹30,000. How many months away is the due date?
questions.explanation: Growth factor=34,500/30,000=1.15, so rt=0.15. With r=0.10, t=1.5 years=18 months.

questions.stem: At 8% simple interest, what is the combined present worth of ₹24,000 due in 6 months and ₹36,000 due in 15 months?
questions.explanation: Present worths are 24,000/1.04 and 36,000/1.10. Their sum is ₹55,804.20.

questions.stem: For a ₹40,000 one-year bill, how much more true discount is obtained at 10% than at 8%?
At 10% per annum, true discount is 4% of the amount due. How many months remain to maturity?
questions.explanation: Let x=rt. Then x/(1+x)=0.04, giving x=1/24. Thus t=(1/24)/0.10=5/12 year=5 months.

questions.stem: A supplier offers ₹4,500 off a ₹1,00,000 invoice due in 6 months. At a 9% simple-interest valuation rate, by how much does this discount exceed the true discount?
A two-year amount due of ₹58,000 has a present worth of ₹50,000 under simple interest. What annual rate is used?
A ₹75,000 payment is due 2 years from issue. It is settled after 8 months. At 9% simple interest, what is its fair settlement value then?
questions.explanation: At settlement, 16 months remain. Value=75,000/[1+0.09×16/12]=₹66,964.29.

questions.stem: A one-year bill has true discount ₹3,150 at 10.5%. What is its present worth?
Two six-month obligations of ₹20,000 and ₹30,000 are valued together at 12%. What is their combined true discount?

What is the true discount on a payment?

**Statement I:** The amount due is ₹54,000.

**Statement II:** Its present worth is ₹50,000.
questions.explanation: True discount is simply amount due minus present worth. Both statements together give ₹4,000; neither alone is enough.

options.label: Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.
Even both statements together are not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.

questions.stem: At 8% per annum, the true discount equals one-eleventh of the amount due. How many months remain to maturity?
At 10%, the true discount on a bill due in one year exceeds the true discount on the same bill due in 6 months by ₹2,000. Find the amount due.
₹54,000 due in one year and ₹60,000 due in two years have the same present worth at simple interest. Find the annual rate.
At 10% simple interest, ₹30,000 due in 6 months and ₹50,000 due in 18 months are replaced by ₹80,000 due in one instalment. After how many months should it be due to preserve present worth?
A contractor may accept ₹50,000 today or ₹56,000 after 15 months. Under simple-interest equivalence, what annual return is implicit in waiting?
questions.explanation: Growth is 12% over 1.25 years. Annual simple rate=12/1.25=9.6%.

questions.stem: A bill discounted 7.5 months before maturity at 10% has true discount ₹2,500. What is its face value?
A ₹1,00,000 payment is originally due in 2 years. Compare its present worth at issue with its settlement value 15 months later, using 8% simple interest. By how much has the value risen?
For an ₹84,000 one-year obligation at 5%, how much larger is simple interest on the amount due than the true discount?
questions.explanation: Interest on face value=₹4,200. True discount=84,000×0.05/1.05=₹4,000. Difference=₹200.

questions.stem: For the same bill, true discount when due in 2 years is 11/6 times the true discount when due in 1 year. What annual simple-interest rate is used?
An ₹80,000 invoice is due in 9 months, but can be settled today for ₹75,000. What annual simple-interest valuation rate makes the two options equivalent?
questions.explanation: The true discount is ₹5,000 on present worth ₹75,000 for 0.75 year. r=5,000/(75,000×0.75)=8.8889%.

questions.stem: Find the total present worth of ₹50,000 due in 6 months at 10%, ₹75,000 due in 2 years at 8%, and ₹1,00,000 due in 3 years at 9%, using simple interest separately for each.
True discount is 20% of present worth for a certain obligation. If the amount due is ₹72,000, find present worth.
questions.explanation: Amount due=PW+TD=1.20PW. Hence PW=72,000/1.20=₹60,000.

questions.stem: A ₹60,000 bill due in one year at a 10% valuation rate has the same present worth as the same amount due after how many months at an 8% rate?
questions.explanation: Equal present worth requires 1+0.10×1 = 1+0.08t. Thus t=1.25 years=15 months.

questions.stem:
What is the time to maturity of a bill?

**Statement I:** The true discount is 6% of present worth.

**Statement II:** The annual simple-interest rate is 8%.
questions.explanation: Statement I gives rt=0.06 but not t; Statement II gives r. Together t=0.06/0.08=0.75 year=9 months.

options.label: Even both statements together are not sufficient.
Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.

questions.stem: At 8% per annum, a payment has present worth ₹40,000 and amount due ₹44,800. In how many months is it due?
questions.explanation: True discount=₹4,800. Since TD=PW×r×t, t=4,800/(40,000×0.08)=1.5 years=18 months.

questions.stem: Two obligations have the same present worth ₹35,000. One is due in 18 months at 11%; the other in 2 years at 7%. How much larger is the first true discount?
questions.explanation: TDs are based on common PW: 35,000×0.11×1.5=₹5,775 and 35,000×0.07×2=₹4,900. Difference=₹875.

questions.stem: At 8% simple interest, what single payment today is equivalent to ₹24,000 due in 6 months, ₹36,000 due in 15 months, and ₹50,000 due in 2 years?
A ₹72,000 liability due in 2 years is replaced by ₹30,000 today and ₹33,000 after 1 year. At what positive simple-interest rate are the plans equivalent?
questions.explanation: Set 30,000+33,000/(1+r)=72,000/(1+2r). Substitution r=0.10 gives 30,000+30,000=60,000 and 72,000/1.20=60,000; solving the resulting quadratic confirms the positive admissible root 10%.

questions.stem: ₹1,00,000 due in one year is valued at 12%. At 10%, after how many months would ₹1,10,000 have the same present worth?
questions.explanation: First PW=1,00,000/1.12. Set 1,10,000/(1+0.10t) equal to this. This gives t=2.32 years=27.84 months.

questions.stem: At one common annual rate, true discount on ₹55,000 due in one year plus true discount on ₹84,000 due in 6 months totals ₹9,000. Find the rate.
questions.explanation: Let r be decimal. Solve 55,000r/(1+r)+84,000(0.5r)/(1+0.5r)=9,000. The positive solution is r=0.10, verified by discounts ₹5,000 and ₹4,000.

questions.stem: What is the present worth of the first payment?
What is the true discount on the second payment?
What is the combined present worth of all three payments?
If the three payments are replaced by one ₹2,76,000 payment, after how many years should it be due to have the same present worth at 8%?
A rectangular electronics enclosure measures 12 cm by 8 cm by 5 cm. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: Volume of a cuboid = 12×8×5 = 480 cm³.

questions.stem: A cube has edge length 6 cm. What is its total surface area?
questions.explanation: Total surface area = 6a² = 6×6² = 216 cm².

questions.stem: A cylinder has radius 5 cm and height 12 cm. Express its volume in terms of π.
questions.explanation: Volume = πr²h = π×25×12 = 300π cm³.

questions.stem: A sphere has radius 3 cm. Express its volume in terms of π.
questions.explanation: Volume = 4/3πr³ = 4/3π×27 = 36π cm³.

questions.stem: A cone has radius 6 cm and height 9 cm. Express its volume in terms of π.
questions.explanation: Volume = 1/3πr²h = 1/3π×36×9 = 108π cm³.

questions.stem: The volume of a cube is 729 cm³. What is its edge length?
questions.explanation: If a³=729, then a=9 cm.

questions.stem: A water tank measures 2 m by 1.5 m by 1 m. What is its capacity in litres?
questions.explanation: Volume=2×1.5×1=3 m³. Since 1 m³=1000 litres, capacity=3000 litres.

questions.stem: A hemispherical dome has radius 7 cm. Express its curved surface area in terms of π.
questions.explanation: Curved surface area of a hemisphere = 2πr² = 2π×49 = 98π cm².

questions.stem: A cylindrical pipe has radius 4 cm and length 10 cm. Express its curved outer surface area in terms of π.
questions.explanation: Curved surface area = 2πrh = 2π×4×10 = 80π cm².

questions.stem: How many cubes of side 5 cm fit exactly in a rectangular box measuring 30 cm by 20 cm by 10 cm?
questions.explanation: The counts along the dimensions are 6,4 and2. Total cubes=6×4×2=48.

questions.stem: What is the space diagonal of a cuboid measuring 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm?
questions.explanation: Diagonal=√(3²+4²+12²)=√169=13 cm.

questions.stem: A solid sphere of radius 6 cm is melted into spheres of radius 2 cm. How many smaller spheres are formed?
questions.explanation: Volumes scale as the cube of radius. Number=(6/2)³=27.

questions.stem: A cylinder has volume 1232 cm³ and radius 7 cm. Find its height using π=22/7.
A cone and a cylinder have the same base radius and height. What is the ratio of their volumes, cone:cylinder?
questions.explanation: Cone volume is one-third of the corresponding cylinder volume, so the ratio is 1:3.

questions.stem: A hollow cylindrical pipe has outer radius 5 cm, inner radius 3 cm and length 14 cm. Find the material volume using π=22/7.
questions.explanation: Material volume=π(R²−r²)h=(22/7)(25−9)14=704 cm³.

questions.stem: A rectangular tank has base dimensions 4 m by 3 m. If it contains 7,200 litres of water, what is the water depth?
questions.explanation: Water volume=7.2 m³. Depth=7.2/(4×3)=0.6 m.

questions.stem: A sphere has radius 5 cm. Express its surface area in terms of π.
questions.explanation: Surface area=4πr²=4π×25=100π cm².

questions.stem: The edge of a cube is increased by 10%. By what percentage does its volume increase?
questions.explanation: Volume scales as the cube of edge. New factor=1.1³=1.331, so the increase is 33.1%.

questions.stem: An open rectangular box has length 10 cm, width 8 cm and height 5 cm. What is its surface area, excluding the top?
questions.explanation: Area=base+four walls=10×8+2×5(10+8)=80+180=260 cm².

questions.stem: A capsule consists of a cylinder of radius 3 cm and length 8 cm with two hemispherical ends. Express its volume in terms of π.
questions.explanation: The two hemispheres form a sphere. Volume=π×3²×8+4/3π×3³=72π+36π=108π cm³.

questions.stem: A conical vessel of radius 6 cm and height 12 cm is full. Its contents are poured into a cylinder of radius 6 cm. What water depth results?
questions.explanation: Cone volume=1/3π×36×12=144π. Cylinder base area=36π, so depth=144π/(36π)=4 cm.

questions.stem: A fully submerged stone displaces 1.5 litres of water. What is the stone’s volume in cubic centimetres?
questions.explanation: A submerged object displaces its own volume. Since 1 litre=1000 cm³, volume=1500 cm³.

questions.stem: All six faces of a cube of edge 10 cm are painted at ₹2 per square centimetre. What is the painting cost?
questions.explanation: Surface area=6×10²=600 cm². Cost=600×₹2=₹1,200.

questions.stem:
What is the volume of a cuboid?

**Statement I:** Its dimensions are in the ratio 2:3:4.

**Statement II:** Its shortest edge is 6 cm.
questions.explanation: Statement I supplies only proportions. Statement II supplies only one length. Together the dimensions are 6,9 and12 cm, so the volume is uniquely determined. Both statements together are sufficient.

options.label: Even both statements together are not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.
Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.

questions.stem: A cone has radius 5 cm and vertical height 12 cm. Express its total surface area in terms of π.
questions.explanation: Slant height=√(5²+12²)=13. Total surface area=πr(l+r)=π×5×18=90π cm².

questions.stem: A sphere of radius 6 cm is recast into identical spheres of radius 3 cm. How many are obtained?
questions.explanation: Number=(6/3)³=8.

questions.stem: A solid consists of a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm topped by a hemisphere of the same radius. Express its volume in terms of π.
questions.explanation: Cylinder volume=490π. Hemisphere volume=2/3π×7³=686π/3. Total=(1470+686)π/3=2156π/3 cm³.

questions.stem: A 44 cm by 22 cm rectangular sheet is rolled into a cylinder in two ways, using each side once as the circumference. What is the ratio of the larger cylinder volume to the smaller?
questions.explanation: If circumference is44, radius=7 and height=22, volume=1078π. If circumference is22, radius=3.5 and height=44, volume=539π. Ratio=2:1.

questions.stem: A sphere is inscribed in a cube. What is the ratio of the cube’s volume to the sphere’s volume?
questions.explanation: Let sphere radius=r, so cube edge=2r. Cube volume=8r³; sphere volume=4πr³/3. Ratio=8:(4π/3)=6:π.

questions.stem: What is the volume of the largest sphere that can fit inside a cube of edge 14 cm?
questions.explanation: The sphere diameter equals the cube edge, so r=7. Volume=4/3π×7³=1372π/3 cm³.

questions.stem: A tank has a 5 m by 4 m base. Its water level rises by 30 cm in 20 minutes under a constant net inflow. What is the net inflow rate?
questions.explanation: Volume increase=5×4×0.30=6 m³=6000 litres. Rate=6000/20=300 litres per minute.

questions.stem: A conical tent has radius 7 m and height 24 m. How much canvas is needed for its curved surface, using π=22/7?
questions.explanation: Slant height=√(7²+24²)=25 m. Curved area=πrl=(22/7)×7×25=550 m².

questions.stem: A solid hemisphere of radius 6 cm is melted into a cone of radius 3 cm. What is the cone’s height?
questions.explanation: Hemisphere volume=2/3π×6³=144π. Cone volume=1/3π×3²×h=3πh. Thus h=48 cm.

questions.stem: A hollow sphere has outer radius 5 cm and inner radius 4 cm. Express the material volume in terms of π.
questions.explanation: Material volume=4/3π(5³−4³)=4/3π(61)=244π/3 cm³.

questions.stem: A frustum of a cone has radii 6 cm and 3 cm and height 8 cm. Express its volume in terms of π.
questions.explanation: Volume=1/3πh(R²+Rr+r²)=1/3π×8(36+18+9)=168π cm³.

questions.stem: A cylinder is cut by a plane parallel to its bases into two cylinders. By how much does the total surface area increase?
questions.explanation: The cut creates two new circular faces, each of area πr². Increase=2πr².

questions.stem: A cube of edge 12 cm is cut into 27 equal smaller cubes. What is the ratio of the total surface area of all small cubes to that of the original cube?
questions.explanation: Each small cube has edge4. Total area=27×6×4²=2592; original area=6×12²=864. Ratio=3:1.

questions.stem:
What is the volume of a right circular cylinder?

**Statement I:** Its curved surface area is 440 cm².

**Statement II:** Its radius is 7 cm, using π=22/7.
questions.explanation: Statement I alone gives only 2πrh. Statement II alone gives only r. Together, 2×22/7×7×h=440 gives h=10 cm, hence the volume is determined. Both statements together are sufficient.

options.label: Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Even both statements together are not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.

questions.stem: A closed cylinder has volume 1000π cm³ and height 10 cm. Express its total surface area in terms of π.
questions.explanation: πr²×10=1000π gives r=10. Total surface area=2πr(h+r)=2π×10×20=400π cm².

questions.stem: A 2 m-long metal pipe has outer radius 5 cm, inner radius 4 cm and density 7.5 g/cm³. Find its mass using π=22/7.
questions.explanation: Length=200 cm. Material volume=(22/7)(25−16)200=39600/7 cm³. Mass=volume×7.5=297000/7 g=42.4286 kg.

questions.stem: A bucket is a frustum with top radius 14 cm, bottom radius 7 cm and height 24 cm. Find its capacity in litres using π=22/7.
A cube of edge 10 cm has a smaller cube of edge 2 cm removed from one corner. What is the total surface area of the remaining solid?
questions.explanation: Three 2×2 squares disappear from the original outer faces, but three equal new cut faces are exposed. The changes cancel, so the surface area remains 6×10²=600 cm².

questions.stem: A closed cylinder has fixed volume 250π cm³. What is its minimum possible total surface area?
questions.explanation: For a closed cylinder of fixed volume, surface area is minimized when h=2r. Then 2πr³=250π, so r=5 and h=10. Minimum area=2πr(r+h)=150π cm².

questions.stem: A sphere is inscribed in a right circular cone of radius 5 cm, height 12 cm and slant height 13 cm. What is the sphere’s radius?
questions.explanation: In the axial triangle, the insphere radius equals area/semiperimeter. Triangle area=5×12=60 and semiperimeter=(10+13+13)/2=18. Radius=60/18=10/3 cm.

questions.stem: A cylindrical vessel of radius 10 cm contains water to a depth of 15 cm. A solid sphere of radius 5 cm is fully submerged without overflow. What is the new water depth?
questions.explanation: Rise=sphere volume/base area=[(4/3)π·5³]/(100π)=5/3 cm. New depth=15+5/3=50/3 cm.

questions.stem: A cone of height 30 cm and base radius 12 cm is cut by a plane parallel to the base 10 cm from its vertex. Express the volume of the resulting frustum in terms of π.
questions.explanation: The removed small cone is similar with scale1/3, so its radius is4. Original volume=1/3π·12²·30=1440π. Small volume=1/3π·4²·10=160π/3. Frustum volume=4160π/3 cm³.

questions.stem: A cube of edge 6 cm is painted on all faces and cut into 216 unit cubes. All small cubes with exactly two painted faces are removed. What volume remains?
questions.explanation: Exactly two painted faces occur on edge cubes excluding corners: 12(6−2)=48 cubes. Remaining unit cubes=216−48=168, so volume=168 cm³.

questions.stem: A solid cone of radius 6 cm and height 12 cm is melted into identical cylinders of radius 2 cm and height 3 cm. How many cylinders are formed?
questions.explanation: Cone volume=1/3π×36×12=144π. Each cylinder volume=π×4×3=12π. Number=144π/12π=12.

questions.stem:
What is the volume of a capsule made from a cylinder with two hemispherical ends?

**Statement I:** The common radius is 3 cm.

**Statement II:** The total end-to-end length is 14 cm.
questions.explanation: Statement I alone does not give cylinder length. Statement II alone does not give radius. Together, cylinder length=14−2×3=8 cm, and the volume is uniquely determined. Both statements together are sufficient.

options.label: Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Even both statements together are not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not sufficient.

questions.stem: A cylindrical hole of radius 3 cm is drilled through the centre of a sphere of radius 6 cm. What is the volume of the remaining “napkin-ring” solid?
questions.explanation: The remaining height is h=2√(6²−3²)=6√3 cm. A napkin ring of height h has volume πh³/6. Therefore volume=π(6√3)³/6=108√3π cm³.

passages.body: A beverage plant has Tank A with 80 litres at 25% syrup and Tank B with 120 litres at 40% syrup. It transfers 20 litres of well-mixed liquid from A to B, mixes B thoroughly, then transfers 20 litres from B back to A. No liquid is lost.
passages.title: Two-tank concentration transfer

passages.body: A rectangular solar field measures 60 m by 40 m. A uniform service strip of width 2 m runs inside all four edges. The remaining inner rectangle is covered by panels. Each panel covers 1.5 m².
passages.title: Solar-field layout

passages.body: A circle of radius 14 cm is divided by two perpendicular diameters into four quadrants. In one quadrant, the chord joining the endpoints of the two radii forms an isosceles right triangle. Use π=22/7 when a numerical value is requested.
passages.title: Quadrant and chord

passages.body: A product team tracks story points completed in eight two-week sprints. The first four sprints record 42, 54, 48 and 56 points. The next three sprints average 60 points. In the eighth sprint, the team completes x points. Management reports that the average over all eight sprints is 55 points. For a reliability metric, the highest and lowest sprint values are removed and the mean of the remaining six is calculated.
passages.title: Sprint velocity caselet

passages.body: A supplier holds three bills: A for ₹1,20,000 due in 4 months, B for ₹80,000 due in 6 months, and C for ₹1,00,000 due in 9 months. A bank discounts all three today at 9% per annum using banker’s discount. Ignore days of grace.
passages.title: Supplier bill-discounting caselet
